summary: Describes the Leighton-Micali hash-based signature system, which builds on work by Lamport, Diffie, Winternitz, and Merkle. It specifies a one-time signature scheme and a general signature scheme that rely only on hash functions, not large-integer math, and are suitable for compact implementations. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Leighton-Micali Signatures (LMS) use hash functions and a tree of one-time signing keys. The signer must keep track of which key has been used and save the updated state before releasing a signature.

what is a stateful signature scheme
subtitle: A stateful digital-signature system built from one-time signatures and hash trees.

tldr.problem: Hash-based signatures provide an alternative to schemes based on large-integer mathematics. They can be compact to implement, but one-time signing keys make the system stateful and require careful tracking.
tldr.mechanism: LM-OTS uses hash chains to sign one message. LMS places many one-time public keys in a Merkle tree, and HSS organizes multiple LMS trees so key generation can be staged.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8554 specifies LM-OTS, LMS, and HSS formats and algorithms as an Informational IRTF document. Reusing a private-key state can remove the security guarantees, so implementations must persist state safely.

facts.label: Hash function in defined parameter sets

today: RFC 8554 is an Informational document from the IRTF's Crypto Forum Research Group. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Hash-Based Digital Signatures
sections.content:
RFC 8554 specifies a digital-signature system based on cryptographic hash functions, following work by Lamport, Diffie, Winternitz, and Merkle as adapted by Leighton and Micali. It defines a one-time signature method and general signature methods built from it.

The RFC describes small private and public keys and fast signing and verification, compared with RSA and ECDSA, alongside large signatures and moderately slow key generation. It says the methods are considered secure against quantum computers according to current knowledge, but emphasizes a practical restriction: the signer must never reuse a one-time private-key state.
sections.plainLanguage: These signature methods use hash functions instead of large-integer mathematics. Their keys change as they are used, so the signer must never reuse a previous key state.

sections.title: LM-OTS: A One-Time Signature
sections.content:
Leighton-Micali One-Time Signature (LM-OTS) signs a hash of the message using a private key made of secret byte strings. The public key is derived by applying a hash function repeatedly to each secret value and hashing the results together.

To sign, the algorithm hashes the message with a randomizer, appends a checksum, and reads the result as a sequence of w-bit values. Each value determines how far to advance a corresponding hash chain; the intermediate chain values form the signature. The verifier completes the chains and checks the resulting public-key value.

The checksum prevents a signer from being forged by advancing hash chains alone: increasing a message digit decreases a checksum digit, which would require reversing a one-way hash chain. The parameter w trades a shorter signature for more hashing work.
sections.plainLanguage: LM-OTS uses message digits to choose positions in several one-way hash chains. A checksum makes it harder to alter the message digits and still produce a valid signature.

sections.title: LMS: A Merkle Tree of One-Time Keys
sections.content:
Leighton-Micali Signatures (LMS) place LM-OTS public keys at the leaves of a perfect binary hash tree. Each parent node is the hash of its two children, and the tree root is the LMS public key. A tree of height h has 2^h leaves.

An LMS signature includes the one-time signature, its leaf number, a typecode, and an authentication path containing the sibling values from that leaf to the root. A verifier reconstructs the path and accepts only if the calculated root matches the known public key.

The private key tracks the next unused leaf. Before releasing a signature, the signer must increment and persist that index; otherwise a crash could cause the same one-time key to sign two messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The LMS public key is the root of a tree containing many one-time public keys. A signature includes enough neighboring tree values for a verifier to rebuild the path from its one-time key to that root.

sections.title: HSS: A Hierarchy of LMS Trees
sections.content:
The Hierarchical Signature System (HSS) links a sequence of LMS trees. The root tree's public key is the HSS public key; each tree signs the next tree's public key, and the lowest-level tree signs the application message.

When a lower-level tree runs out of one-time keys, the signer generates a replacement tree and has the level above sign its public key. If the root key is exhausted, the HSS key pair must not generate more signatures. The RFC allows one to eight levels and says a parameter set must not change at a given level.

HSS reduces the amount of key generation needed before the public key is ready, because only the root tree must be generated initially. Its signatures are larger and verification takes longer than for a single LMS tree.
sections.plainLanguage: HSS uses higher-level trees to authenticate new lower-level trees as they are needed. This can reduce initial key-generation work, but it adds signatures that verifiers must check.

sections.title: Security and Persistent State
sections.content:
The RFC requires verifiers to check all typecodes and reject unknown or mismatched types and objects of the wrong length. It states a security result for LMS under assumptions about the number of keys and hash computations, while cautioning developers about state management.

The signer must ensure that an updated private-key index reaches nonvolatile storage before releasing a signature. File-system and device caches can delay writes, so implementations may need system-specific steps to make persistence reliable. For hierarchical signatures, the RFC recommends keeping the second-level private key only in memory when possible, so it can be regenerated after a restart.
sections.plainLanguage: The signer must record that a one-time key has been used before giving out its signature. If a restart makes the signer reuse that key, an attacker may be able to forge another message.
